title: 2020 AMC 10A Problem 18
statement: Let \((a,b,c,d)\) be an ordered quadruple of not necessarily distinct integers, each one of them in the set \(\{0,1,2,3\}.\) For how many such quadruples is it true that \(a\cdot d-b\cdot c\) is odd? (For example, \((0,3,1,1)\) is one such quadruple, because \(0\cdot 1-3\cdot 1 = -3\) is odd.)

solutions.text:
Only parity matters. Modulo \(2\), the condition is that \(ad-bc\) is \(1\), meaning the matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}\) is invertible over \(\mathbb F_2\).

There are \((4-1)(4-2)=6\) invertible \(2\times2\) matrices over \(\mathbb F_2\). Each parity pattern lifts to \(2^4=16\) choices from \(\{0,1,2,3\}\), so there are \(6\cdot16=96\) quadruples. Thus, C is the correct answer.
hints: Count invertible \(2\times2\) matrices over the two-element field
